title: Marathon Training Plan for Women: What to Adjust
excerpt: What women should adjust in marathon training (menstrual cycle, iron, fueling, strength, pregnancy and postpartum) and which week-by-week plan to follow.
body:
Marathon Training Plan for Women: What to Adjust

Women don't need a separate marathon schedule. The same principles apply: gradual mileage, a long run that builds, mostly easy running and a proper taper. What can differ is how you handle your menstrual cycle, iron, fueling, bone health and strength work, and pregnancy or postpartum if that applies to you. This page covers what to adjust and which of our week-by-week plans to follow.

Which plan should you follow?

Pick the plan that matches your current running, not your gender:

  • First marathon, running about 3 times a week: 18-week beginner plan.
  • Low base or returning to running (including after pregnancy, once you're cleared): 6 month plan.
  • Have run a half, about 20 miles a week: 20 week plan.
  • Solid base of 25–30 miles a week: 16 week plan.
  • Breaking four hours: sub 4 hour plan.
  • Experienced marathoner: intermediate plan.
  • Only three days a week: 3 day a week plan.

To compare them side by side, see our plan comparison table.

Training through your menstrual cycle

Research on how cycle phase affects performance is mixed, and the differences between individuals are larger than any average effect. The practical approach is to track your cycle alongside your training for a couple of months and look for your own patterns.

  • If you consistently feel flat at a certain point in your cycle, swap your hard session to another day that week.
  • Body temperature runs slightly higher in the second half of the cycle, so pay extra attention to hydration and heat on long runs.
  • Note where race day falls in your cycle, and plan practical items such as period products in advance.

Missed or stopped periods during heavy training are not a normal side effect of training. They can signal low energy availability, which harms bone health. See a doctor if this happens.

Iron

Female runners are at higher risk of low iron, because of menstrual losses plus the extra demands of endurance training. Common signs include unusual fatigue, breathlessness at easy paces, and paces that stop improving despite training. Ask your doctor for a ferritin test before or early in your training block. Don't take iron supplements without testing: too much iron is also harmful. Iron-rich foods such as red meat, beans, lentils and fortified cereals, eaten with vitamin C, help with absorption.

Fueling enough

Marathon training raises your energy needs considerably, and under-fueling is common. Eat a carbohydrate-based meal or snack before key sessions, refuel within an hour of long runs, and don't try to lose weight during peak training. Calcium and vitamin D support the bone health that high mileage depends on. Our guide to marathon fueling covers carbohydrate targets for long runs and race week.

Strength training

Two short strength sessions a week reduce injury risk and support bone density. Good choices include squats, lunges, deadlifts, calf raises and single-leg work. Pelvic floor exercises are worth adding, especially if you notice leaking on long runs. That is common, but not something you have to put up with: a women's health physiotherapist can help.

Pregnancy and postpartum

Many people keep running during an uncomplicated pregnancy, but training for and racing a marathon while pregnant is a decision to make with your doctor or midwife, who knows your situation. After giving birth, return to running gradually, only once you have been cleared, and ideally with guidance from a pelvic health physiotherapist. Rebuild your base with walking and easy running before starting any marathon plan. The 6 month plan is a sensible way back.

Kit

A well-fitted, high-support sports bra and anti-chafe balm matter more over 26.2 miles than any other kit. Test everything you plan to race in during your longest training runs.

FAQ

Should women train differently for a marathon?

The training structure is the same. The differences are in monitoring and support: tracking your cycle, checking iron, fueling enough, and strength work for bone health. Choose a plan based on your current mileage and goal.

Can I train for a marathon while pregnant?

Talk to your doctor or midwife. Continuing exercise you already do is often encouraged in an uncomplicated pregnancy, but a full marathon training block and race need individual medical advice.

Does my period affect marathon training?

For some runners it does, and for others not noticeably. Track how you feel across a few cycles and move hard sessions if you see a consistent pattern. Missed periods are a reason to see a doctor.

Do female runners need more iron?

Often, yes. Female endurance runners have a higher risk of low iron. Get your ferritin tested, and only supplement on medical advice.
keyTakeaway: Women follow the same marathon training principles; what changes is monitoring cycle, iron and fueling, adding strength work for bone health, and getting medical advice around pregnancy.
